figures.caption: Figure 1: The concept generalization setting and the encoder-decoder asymmetry. (a) Images containing C are removed only from the target subject’s training set and not from other subjects; the model is evaluated only on images containing C. (b) The encoder retains most of its concept-specific recall under this holdout, while the MindEye2 decoder (Scotti et al., 2024) loses most of it. Encoder recall is measured by decoding its predicted fMRI with a MindEye2 trained with C present and with additional synthetic data (See Sec. 6 for more details).

Figure 2: Encoder-generated synthetic fMRI for decoder training. The encoder is first pretrained and fine-tuned to the target subject (step 1), applied to a new pool of images to generate synthetic fMRI (step 2), and the synthetic pairs are added to the decoder’s training set (step 3).

Table 1: Concept generalization for decoders. Decoders are trained with/without C for the target subject and evaluated on images containing C. Adding synthetic data improves generalization towards C. Bold marks the better of the two unseen variants, with or without synthetic data.

Figure 3: Qualitative reconstruction highlights. We show the ground truth image and the corresponding reconstructions for each decoder, before or after adding synthetic data to training. While the baseline model fails to accurately reconstruct C, the synthetic variant is able to recover it.

Figure 4: Effect of synthetic data across data scales. The x axis is in log scale. ρ denotes the fitted data-efficiency gain. We show 4 metrics spanning the metric groups; the rest are in Appendix E.3.

Table 2: Encoder variants as synthetic-data sources (supercategory generalization). Variants differ in whether C was available during cross-subject pre-training and target-subject adaptation (Target). Probe decoder: a from-scratch MindEye2 trained on real data plus that encoder’s synthetic pairs, evaluated on images containing C; the two oracle variants see real responses to C and cannot be used for synthesis. Encoder: Pearson r of the predicted fMRI, and decoded recall / decoded relaxed recall (D.Rec. / D.Rel.) of images reconstructed from it.

Table 3: Size of each concept C. The 12 COCO supercategories used for supercategory generalization, each followed by the two categories (indented) used for category generalization. Person has no underlying category. Train counts are out of 9,000 images per subject and test counts out of 1,000. Note that each image may contain several categories.

Table 4: Concept generalization for decoders, evaluated on unrelated images. Decoders are trained with/without C and evaluated on images that do not contain C. Removing C’s training data or adding synthetic data shifts these scores by an order of magnitude less than on images containing C; see Appendix C.1 and Table 19.

Table 5: Concept generalization for decoders: low-level metrics. Same models and evaluation images as Table 1: decoders are trained with/without C for the target subject and evaluated on images containing C. Bold marks the better of the two unseen variants, with or without synthetic data.

Table 6: Encoder impact on decoding performance by training condition, concept generalization: low-level metrics. Same models and evaluation images as Tables 2 and 10. Each row trains a MindEye2 decoder from scratch, varying the encoder that generated its synthetic pairs. The last row of each panel uses real fMRI for C as an upper bound.

Table 8: Encoder retention with a real-data-only readout. Subject 1, C = animal. Encoderpredicted test fMRI is decoded by a MindEye2 readout trained with C present on real data only. Retained is the ratio to the oracle of the same family (Recall / Relaxed Recall). The last row is the probe decoder of Sec. 6 on real test fMRI, relative to its own C-seen model (Table 12).

Table 9: Synthetic-data controls and frozen-backbone encoders. MindEye2 probe decoder trained from scratch on subject 1, supercategory generalization (12 concepts). Both controls use identical synthetic fMRI, predicted for images not containing C; they differ only in whether it is paired with those images (non-C images) or with the C images (wrong fMRI). Frozen encoders keep DINOv2 fixed instead of LoRA-tuning it. The last row uses real fMRI for C as an upper bound.

Table 10: Encoder variants and their value as synthetic-data sources, category generalization (22 concepts). Same layout as Table 2. Bold marks the best of the three synthesis encoders in each probe-decoder column.

Table 12: Encoder designs as synthetic-data sources. MindEye2 probe decoder trained with synthetic data from each encoder, subject 1, C = animal. Gap rec. is (syn − unseen)/(seen − unseen) for Recall / Relaxed Recall. The first two rows are the probe decoder trained with real fMRI for C and without synthetic data. OpenCLIP denotes the OpenCLIP ViT-bigG backbone.

Table 13: Decoding encoder-predicted test fMRI under the holdout. Subject 1, C = animal; Incep / CLIP of images reconstructed from each encoder’s predictions by the fixed MindEye2 readout of Sec. 6. Within-concept identification is defined in Appendix D.5. The OpenCLIP UE uses OpenCLIP ViT-bigG, the same backbone as SynBrain.
Table 16: Effect of synthetic data across data scales. Numbers correspond to values from Figures 4 and 6. The better result within each decoder pair in bold.

Figure 5: Encoder pre-training matters most when target-subject data is scarce. Improvement of synthetic data for MindEye2 over its real-data-only baseline, on all eight metrics, when the synthetic data come from a cross-subject pre-trained encoder (blue) versus an encoder trained from scratch on the target subject (orange). Both help at every budget, but the pre-trained encoder’s advantage is largest at small budgets and shrinks as target-subject data grows (Appendix G.5). SSIM is the exception, with small gains and no consistent ordering between the two encoders.
Figure 6: Effect of synthetic data across data scales: remaining metrics. Companion to Figure 4, showing SSIM, AlexNet(2), Inception and SwAV for each decoder.

Figure 7: Scaling the amount of synthetic data. Improvement over the baseline for MindEye2, as a function of the number of synthetic image-fMRI pairs added per real training image. One line per real-data budget x; each curve is measured against its own x-matched m=0 baseline, so all curves start at zero. Lower-is-better metrics are sign-flipped, so up is better in every panel; note that vertical scales differ across panels. Gains are positive at every budget, and grow as the real-data budget shrinks.
Table 17: Extension to video decoding. A NEURONS model is trained with and without synthetic fMRI, for limited and full data settings. Bold marks the better of the two conditions for each budget.

Table 18: Fraction of the concept generalization gap recovered by synthetic data, (syn − unseen)/(seen − unseen) on aggregate means, with 95% bootstrap CIs over the 48 subjectsupercategory cells. Left: the three decoders of Table 1. Right: the probe decoder of Table 2 under each synthesis encoder. SSIM is omitted because the holdout barely changes it. Subject-level bootstrap intervals are similar and are provided with the released results.

Table 19: Effect of the training-set manipulations on images that do not contain C, compared with their effect on images that do. ∆C and ∆¬C are mean paired differences over the 48 subject-concept cells on the concept test set (Table 1) and the complementary test set (Table 4); positive = improvement, EffNet and SwAV sign-flipped, identification metrics in percentage points. Ratio is ∆¬C/∆C . ∗ marks ∆¬C significant after Holm correction (Wilcoxon signed-rank, 16 comparisons per decoder).
